content:

Wine Communicators of Australia (WCA) has announced the finalists of the 2026 Wine Communicator Awards across its thirteen individual categories.

“Each year we turn a spotlight on those Wine Communicators who are doing outstanding work promoting, educating and engaging the wider public on the wonders of wine. The finalists this year all sent in fantastic submissions which showed the genuine depth and breadth of excellence in Australian wine communication,” said Ruth Harris, WCA’s executive officer.

“They included insightful wine books and articles; entertaining podcasts and YouTube channels; brilliant brand marketing campaigns; top quality wine educators; successful wine tasting events — big and small; beautifully-designed websites and wine packaging; and fabulous cellar-door, sales and marketing people promoting wine with passion. Judging involved detailed scrutiny to determine who was worthy of being named a finalist and confirms each of the named finalists as inspiring examples of wine communication excellence.”

WCA said each submission was reviewed by a panel of independent, expert judges. The winners of each category and the overall 2026 Wine Communicator of the Year, who is chosen by the WCA Board from the category winners, will be revealed at the Wine Communicator Awards Ceremony on Thursday 5 November 2026 in Sydney.

content:
Society’s Lee Sangyeop, Loïc Avril, and Yuki Hirose MS were awarded the prestigious Judy Hirst Award. Image credit Marie-Luise Skibbe

The results of Australia’s Wine List of the Year Awards are in, and Melbourne venue Society has been crowned ‘Australia’s Wine List of the Year’. Celebrating its 33rd Anniversary, the Awards ceremony was presented at NSW Parliament House in Sydney where more than 300 industry figures gathered on Monday 28 September.

In addition to the major trophy, Society also picked up another three major titles including ‘Australia’s Best Capital City Dining Wine List’, ‘Best Wine List Victoria’ and ‘Australia’s Best List of Wines by the Glass’. The venue was also a finalist in another three categories: ‘Australia’s Best Listing of Victorian Wines’, ‘Australia’s Best Listing of New Zealand Wines’ and ‘Australia’s Best Listing of Cellared and Museum Wines’. Society’s head sommeliers Loïc Avril, Yuki Hirose MS and sommelier Lee Sangyeop were awarded the prestigious ‘Judy Hirst Award’, which is awarded to the sommeliers responsible for the winning list.

Society’s winning list was praised by chair of judges Toni Paterson MW for its impressive range and versatile offering to cater for those looking for something familiar or new.

“This ranks among Australia’s and the world’s great wine lists, exceptional in its vintage depth and curation and broad in both local and international scope. At heart, it’s a celebration of quality in all its forms,” said Paterson.

“There are close to 90 wines by the glass, ranging from well-priced Australian favourites like MMAD Vineyard Chenin through premium local Chardonnay from By Farr and Tolpuddle to icon reds including Mount Mary Pinot, The Armagh and Grange poured from magnums. Rarities from further afield, including the likes of Benjamin Leroux 1er Cru Meursault or Domaine de la Pousse d’Or Chambolle-Musigny Les Amoureuses, are available as a taste, half-pour or glass.”

Front runners and Hall of Fame inductees

Other front runners for this year’s awards include Perth’s Gibney which was awarded ‘Best Wine List WA’; ‘Australia’s Best Digestif List’, and ‘The Peter Forrestal Award’ for ‘Australia’s Best Listing of Western Australian Wines’. Gibney was also a finalist for four categories including the major title of ‘Australia’s Wine List of the Year 2026’ with judges noting the list’s depth and balance of well-known and up-and-coming producers. Sydney’s Altitude Restaurant at the Shangri-La also took home three titles with judges praising the comprehensive list that also highlights some “left-of-centre” options for those looking to explore.

This year’s state and territory stand-outs included The Boat House (‘Best Wine List ACT’); Shell House Dining Room & Terrace (‘Best Wine List NSW’); Otto Brisbane (‘Best Wine List QLD’); 2KW Bar + Restaurant (‘Best Wine List SA’); and Black Cow Bistro (‘Best Wine List TAS’). It’s the first time Shell House Dining Room & Terrace and 2KW Bar + Restaurant have taken out these major category wins.

“Despite recent challenges, our restaurant sector has great energy, with fabulous wine and beverage lists compiled by confident, knowledgeable sommeliers,” said Paterson of this year’s results.

“The best lists are showing greater support for Australian wines, including those from their home state, which is heartening, especially when local wines represent excellent value, are better than ever, and offer great style and varietal diversity.

“This year has seen the rise of Grenache, mini-cocktails, chilled reds and small pours by the glass, the latter encouraging experimentation while staying mindful of cost. The international offering is incredibly varied, allowing people to explore the world of wine without leaving our shores. We have also seen a wider range of cuisines and menu formats, with share plates increasingly popular.”

Eight venues were also added to the ‘Australia’s Wine List of the Year Awards – Hall of Fame’. To be applicable, venues must have won ‘Australia’s Wine List of the Year’ once or a State/Territory or Australian category award three times while also maintaining their glass rating each year. Among the new inductees for 2026 were Circl (‘Australia’s Wine List of the Year’); Agnes (‘Best Listing of Queensland Wines’ in 2023, 2024, 2025); Fico (‘Best Listing of Tasmanian Wines’ in 2021, 2022, 2025); Settlers Tavern (‘Best Country Restaurant’ in 2022, 2023, 2025); Woodcut (‘Best Hotel List’ in 2023, 2024, 2025); Society (‘Best Listing of French Wines’ in 2023, 2024, 2025); Hardy’s Verandah Restaurant (‘Best Listing of South Australian Wines’ in 2017, 2021, 2025).

Additionally, Amanda Yallop of Fink Group was added to the Hall of Fame. The award is presented periodically to “recognise an outstanding individual and their contribution to industry education, the service of fine wine and the standard of wine lists within the Australian hospitality and tourism industries over recent times”. She is only the third individual in 33 years to receive this honour, joining David Lawler (2018) and Franck Moreau MS (2014).

Founded in 1993

The awards were established in 1993 by Rob Hirst OAM and his late wife, Judy, after whom the main award is named, together with Tucker Seabrook. The awards honour the time, skill, and resources that go into developing the highest-quality wine lists and pay tribute to the talented sommeliers, owners, their teams and the cellars behind them.

“It is wonderful to see the outstanding level of support for the Australia’s Wine List of the Year Awards again this year and the recognition that they deliver to those in the industry continuing to pursue excellence with the list they present to their customers. The quality of wine lists across the country has never been better,” said Hirst.

“These awards are about the recognition and celebration of the outstanding commitment, work and investment of the sommeliers, owners, beverage directors, venue managers and entrepreneurs who make Australia’s hospitality industry one of the best in the world. We congratulate all award winners and glass-rated venues for their achievements this year.”

State highlights

Award organisers have compiled a list of state-by-state highlights:

NSW

New South Wales continued its strong presence in the Awards with a total of 16 major category wins. Altitude Restaurant led the way for the state with three major category wins for ‘Australia’s Best Listing of NSW Wines’, ‘Australia’s Best Listing of Organic and Biodynamic Wines’, and ‘Australia’s Best Hotel/Resort Dining Wine List’. It was also a finalist for ‘Australia’s Best Listing of ACT and Canberra District Wines’ and ‘Australia’s Best Listing of Australian Wines’.

Newcomer Infinity by Mark Best made an impressive debut with two wins: ‘Australia’s Best Listing of Australian Wines’ and ‘The Tony Hitchin Award for Australia’s Best New Wine List’. Hall of Fame member Jonah’s Restaurant and Boutique Hotel continued to make its mark by winning ‘Australia’s Best Food & Wine Matching List’ and the consumer-voted ‘Australia’s Choice Award’.

Shell House Dining Room & Terrace won the overall Award for ‘Best Wine List NSW’, while inner-west favourite ANTE made its debut through the title of ‘Australia’s Best List of Japanese Sake’. Olympus Dining was awarded ‘Australia’s Best Listing of Greek Wines’ for the second year running, and Devine Food & Wine won ‘Australia’s Best Aperitif’ for the third time, previously winning in 2018 and 2024.

Other highlights include Hall of Fame members Rockpool Bar & Grill Sydney acknowledged with ‘Australia’s Best Listing of Cellared and Museum Wines’; The Rover being awarded ‘Australia’s Best Wine List’ (max. 50 Wines) and Me-Gal being named ‘Australia’s Best Wine List’ (max. 100 Wines).

VIC

Victorian venues took out a total of 10 major categories, with Society leading the way through its overall win alongside its titles of ‘Australia’s Best Capital City Dining Wine List’; ‘Best Wine List Victoria’ and ‘Australia’s Best List of Wines by the Glass’. The Mornington Peninsula’s Ten Minutes by Tractor added to its successful history with the Awards by winning ‘Australia’s Best Champagne List’ and ‘Australia’s Best Listing of Victorian Wines’.

Another Mornington Peninsula local, Laura at Pt. Leo Estate, was acknowledged with the title of ‘Australia’s Best Country/Regional Dining Wine List’. Last year’s winner of the ‘Tony Hitchin Award’, Maison Bâtard, was awarded ‘Australia’s Best Listing of French Wines’. Florentino marked its first entry under the stewardship of Edition Hospitality with the win of ‘Australia’s Best Listing of Italian Wines’ while sister venue Reine & La Rue was acknowledged with ‘Australia’s Best Listing of USA Wines’.

WA

Perth’s beachside brasserie Gibney continued its dominance as top performer for the West by taking out ‘Best Wine List WA’; ‘Australia’s Best Digestif List’, and ‘The Peter Forrestal Award for Australia’s Best Listing of Western Australian Wines’. It was also a finalist for four categories including the major title of ‘Australia’s Wine List of the Year 2026’, ‘Australia’s Best Capital City Dining Wine List’, ‘Australia’s Best Champagne List’, and ‘Australia’s Best Cocktail List’.

West Leederville’s neighbourhood pub Besk celebrated back-to-back wins for the title of ‘Australia’s Best Beer List’. Foni Pollitt of Hall of Famers Mayfair Lane Pub & Dining Room was acknowledged by her peers to be awarded the ‘Sommelier’s Choice Award’.

SA

South Australia’s charge was led by The Crafers Hotel which was awarded ‘Australia’s Best Pub Dining Wine List’ and ‘Australia’s Best Listing of South Australian Wine’. 2KW Bar & Restaurant were crowned ‘Best Wine List SA’, with judge Andrew Graham praising the list’s Local Heroes; selection championing cult-status SA producers alongside the up-and-coming.

Adelaide CBD haunt A Prayer for the Wild at Heart received ‘Australia’s Best Wine List’ (max. 200 Wines) for the second year running, while Restaurant Botanic continued its streak of ‘Australia’s Best Non-Alcoholic List’ by winning it for the third year in a row.

Other highlights include CBD venue Canopy acknowledged with ‘Australia’s Best Cocktail List’ plus the Clare Valley’s The Rising Sun made its debut with the title of ‘Australia’s Best Listing of a Single Region’s Wines’.

TAS

Launceston’s Black Cow Bistro received the award for ‘Best Wine List TAS’ with judges noting its diversity in producers and varieties across The Apple Isle. The Agrarian Kitchen in New Norfolk continued its respected celebration of Tasmanian produce by securing the Award for ‘Australia’s Best Listing of Tasmanian Wines’ for the second year in a row and also being named as a finalist for ‘Best Wine List TAS’.

Hobart restaurant Fico was acknowledged as a finalist for ‘Best Wine List TAS’, ‘Australia’s Best Sparkling Wine List’ and ‘Australia’s Best Listing of Tasmanian Wines’. Fellow Hobart local Peppina was also named a finalist for ‘Australia’s Best Hotel/Resort Dining Wine List’ and ‘Best Wine List TAS’.

QLD

Following its six inductions into the Australia’s Wine List of the Year Awards Hall of Fame last year, Cru Bar + Cellar continued its dominance by being named ‘Australia’s Best Sparkling Wine List’ and ‘Australia’s Best Listing of New Zealand’. The Fortitude Valley favourite was also a finalist for ‘Australia’s Best Listing of USA Wines’.

Fink Group’s Otto Brisbane was awarded the overall title of ‘Best Wine List QLD’, while Hall of Famers Blackbird Brisbane was named ‘Australia’s Best Listing of Queensland Wine’ for the second year in a row and a finalist for ‘Australia’s Best Listing of Organic and Biodynamic Wines’.

ACT

Canberran Italian restaurant Capitol Bar & Grill celebrated its win as ‘Australia’s Best Listing of ACT and Canberra District Wines’ for the third consecutive year with judges noting its breadth of local producers from across eight regions. Following its induction into the Hall of Fame last year, The Boat House was awarded the title of ‘Best Wine List ACT’ for its thoughtful selection of benchmarks and newcomers from the area.

The Riesling-led wine bar Rizla was also acknowledged as a finalist for ‘Australia’s Best Wine List’ (max. 200 Wines) and ‘Australia’s Best Listing of ACT and Canberra District Wines’.

content:
The symposium told a consistent message: for businesses and individuals to focus on practical actions within their control. Image credit Robyn Strathearn Photography

Earlier this month, more than 200 professionals from across Australia’s grape and wine community gathered in Melbourne for the 2026 Australian Women in Wine National Symposium, which confronted workforce, leadership and gender-equity challenges as well as shared practical ideas for building a stronger, more inclusive and sustainable industry.

Held under the theme ‘Rising Together – Shaping What Comes Next’, the sell-out event brought together industry leaders, business owners, winemakers, growers, researchers and emerging professionals “to examine the people and leadership challenges facing the sector”.

Organisers said that the conversations were against a backdrop of persistent gender disparities across Australian wine.

According to Wine Australia data, while university wine intakes are close to evenly split between women and men, women represent only around 30% of the sector overall. In key technical roles, the gap is even wider, with women accounting for just 16.7% of winemakers and 21.5% of viticulturists nationally.

Pay disparities also persist, with figures presented during the symposium showing that the average female winemaker earns around $14,000 less per year than the average male winemaker, while female viticulturists earn around $18,000 less per year.

A consistent message emerged throughout the day: “while many of the pressures facing Australian wine are complex, there are practical actions businesses and individuals can take now”.

Australian Women in Wine (AWIW) chair Rachel Triggs said the symposium demonstrated the value of bringing the industry together to move from discussion to practical action.

“What stood out throughout the day was the determination to move beyond talking about the challenges and focus on what we can actually do next.

“Women are entering wine education in almost equal numbers, yet we are still losing too many from the industry before they progress into technical, senior and leadership roles. That tells us the challenge is not simply attracting women to wine, but creating the conditions that allow them to build sustainable, rewarding careers.

“Whether it is leadership, flexibility, workplace culture or opening up new opportunities, meaningful change comes from turning good intentions into practical action,” she said.

Carolyn Creswell, Carman’s Kitchen founder and CEO, was a keynote speaker at the event who challenged delegates to remain customer-focused, create space for innovation and difficult conversations, protect their time and question outdated ways of working.

Her message included a reminder that one of the most dangerous phrases in business is ‘we’ve always done it this way’, and that effective strategy is as much about deciding what not to do, as to what to pursue.

Conversations emphasised the importance of moving beyond policies and commitments to practical implementation. Structural approaches to gender equity, alternative working models including job sharing, and the role supportive workplace cultures can play in attracting and retaining talent were explored throughout discussions.

Lucy Du, representing Global Victoria, spoke about the importance of access to markets, networks, opportunities and decision-making, as well as the value different perspectives and lived experiences bring to leadership. She also highlighted the growing importance of women as consumers in China and the opportunities available to Victorian wine businesses seeking to build international connections.

Closing keynote speaker, Mind Insurance Founder and CEO Mel Neil, focused on “navigating uncertainty by identifying what sits outside our control and where we can have influence”. Delegates were encouraged to direct their energy towards meaningful action, while recognising the role emotional intelligence plays alongside technical capability in leadership, decision-making and team performance, particularly during periods of pressure, change and uncertainty.

The women behind the event

LTR: Luisa Alemao, Lynda Schenk and Chloé James of Purple Giraffe.

Organisers shared exclusively to Daily Wine News that a key force behind the symposium’s success was the partnership between Australian Women in Wine and marketing consultants Purple Giraffe.

Purple Giraffe worked alongside the AWIW team to manage the strategic marketing, communications and event delivery, including coordinating speakers, sponsorship support, stakeholder communications and assets.

Purple Giraffe shared that the project was “an opportunity to apply our strategic marketing expertise to a cause closely aligned with PG’s values: supporting women, leadership and positive change”.

AWIW director Ali Lockwood said the organisation couldn’t have delivered “such a polished, professional and successful event” without the Purple Giraffe team, including marketing consultant Chloé James who led the project.

“From day one, Chloé stepped in with very little notice, quickly got up to speed and took ownership of every detail. Even when things became challenging behind the scenes, she remained calm, organised and completely in control, ensuring everything ran smoothly from start to finish. Beyond her exceptional professionalism, Chloé was an absolute pleasure to work with. Her positive attitude, responsiveness and commitment to excellence made all the difference.

“We were incredibly fortunate to have both Chloé and Purple Giraffe supporting us. Thank you to Chloé, Lynda and the entire Purple Giraffe team for helping make our event such a success.”

title: SA Govt establishes $8m primary industries research and innovation fund
summary:
The South Australian Government has established an $8 million research and innovation fund for the state’s primary production and forestry sectors, including the wine industry. The Primary Industries Future Forward Fund will be delivered over four years and support industry-led projects across forestry, livestock, dairy, grains, horticulture, wine, spirits, seafood and fisheries. The fund will support research and innovation aimed at increasing productivity and capability, building the capacity of primary producers to respond to environmental and market pressures, improving sustainability throughout supply chains, strengthening the primary industries workforce, and improving preparedness for environmental disruptions, biosecurity threats and other emerging issues. The government said projects should also align with relevant industry masterplans, blueprints or other strategic plans and reports, including the South Australian Wine Industry Association’s Key Priorities 2025-2028 and the Wine Grape Council SA Strategic Plan 2025-2027.

content:
The South Australian Government has established an $8 million research and innovation fund for the state’s primary production and forestry sectors, including the wine industry.

The Primary Industries Future Forward Fund will be delivered over four years and support industry-led projects across forestry, livestock, dairy, grains, horticulture, wine, spirits, seafood and fisheries.

The fund will support research and innovation aimed at increasing productivity and capability, building the capacity of primary producers to respond to environmental and market pressures, improving sustainability throughout supply chains, strengthening the primary industries workforce, and improving preparedness for environmental disruptions, biosecurity threats and other emerging issues.

The government said projects should also align with relevant industry masterplans, blueprints or other strategic plans and reports, including the South Australian Wine Industry Association’s Key Priorities 2025-2028 and the Wine Grape Council SA Strategic Plan 2025-2027.

Australian Wine Research Institute managing director Dr Mark Krstic said innovation is important for the South Australian wine industry as it responds to difficult market conditions.

“The wine industry globally is facing significant headwinds at present. Investing in innovation is key to supporting the South Australian wine industry to adapt and thrive again in these challenging market conditions.

“The South Australian Government has a strong history of backing its primary producers to develop and adopt world-leading science and industry innovations.”

The $8 million Future Forward Fund is additional to the South Australian Government’s $50 million Research and Productivity Fund included in the 2026-27 state budget, with the Future Forward Fund specifically targeted at primary industries and forestry.

South Australian Minister for Primary Industries and Regional Development Clare Scriven said the fund is intended to support industry-led research and innovation.

“The Primary Industries Future Forward Fund is about backing agricultural research and innovation that is industry-led and aimed at advancing primary production and forestry in our state.”

The fund follows the 150th anniversary of the invention of the stump-jump plough by Yorke Peninsula brothers Richard and Clarence Smith, which the government describes as an example of South Australia’s history of agricultural innovation.

Applications and guidelines for the Primary Industries Future Forward Fund are available at pir.sa.gov.au/future-forward-fund.

content:
Venues across Tasmania have been named finalists in the 2026 Tasmanian Wine List of the Year awards, presented by Wine Tasmania.

The 17 finalists include restaurants, wine bars, pubs, accommodation venues and specialist retailers, with venues represented across the state from Geeveston to Stanley and from Strahan to Swansea.

The annual awards recognise venues for their representation of Tasmanian wine, with judges assessing the breadth and representation of Tasmanian wines on offer, how each list is put together and how effectively venues present the state’s producers and regions.

Wine Tasmania CEO Sheralee Davies congratulated this year’s finalists.

“The standard of entries this year was exceptional and the pride in our local wines is so gratifying to see. With several new entrants, this year’s finalists represent the most diverse group in the nine years of the program,” Davies said.

“What we love about these awards is that there’s no single formula for a great Tasmanian wine list. It might be a beautifully curated restaurant list, a cracking selection at the local pub, a small wine bar pouring something unexpected, or a retailer helping customers discover a new favourite. These finalists are spread right across the island, from Geeveston to Stanley and from Strahan to Swansea. Each has its own approach, but they all share a genuine enthusiasm for Tasmanian wine and the talented people who grow and make it.”

Public voting is now open for the 2026 People’s Choice Award, giving consumers the opportunity to vote for their preferred finalist venue. Everyone who votes will also go into the draw to win 12 mixed bottles of Tasmanian wine.

The People’s Choice Award sits alongside the independently judged categories of Best Wine List – Hobart, Best Wine List – Launceston, Best Regional Wine List, Best Small Wine Bar List, and the overall Tasmanian Wine List of the Year.

Public voting for the People’s Choice Award closes Friday 30th October, with votes able to be submitted at winetasmania.com.au/vote. Winners of the 2026 Tasmanian Wine List of the Year awards will be announced from Monday 2 November 2026.

content:
New Zealand Winegrowers (NZW) has released its 2026 Annual Report, with exports reaching $2.108 billion and export volume increasing to 306.2 million litres in the 12 months to June 2026.

NZW said the result “reflects an overall sales increase of 8% driven by export growth and represents the industry’s second-highest June year total on record”.

“In the face of a challenging global and domestic environment, New Zealand wine continued to outperform the wider category in key markets, providing grounds for confidence in the long-term prospects of New Zealand wine,” it said.

Meanwhile, individual businesses across the sector were making adjustments. Vintage 2026 delivered a smaller harvest of approximately 440,000 tonnes, down a significant 15% on the previous year, bringing production “into closer balance with current market demand and supporting the industry’s focus on sustainable long-term growth”.

Fabian Yukich, chair of New Zealand Winegrowers, said the report showed an industry that was far from standing still.

“This has been a challenging year across the global wine industry, but New Zealand wine continues to show remarkable resilience.

“What stands out is the determination of growers and wineries to adapt. Businesses in the sector are making adjustments, the progress made this year gives us confidence that it is moving towards a more balanced footing”.

Yukich added that the report demonstrated the sector’s resilience.

“Consumers around the world continue to discover, love and buy New Zealand wines. Our focus is on supporting members through the immediate challenges while continuing to strengthen the opportunities that will carry the industry forward.”

CEO Anishka Jelicich, who was appointed to the role in July, said the Annual Report marked the start of the next phase for NZW, guided by its new strategy.

“Our new strategy has a clear purpose: to elevate and sustain the New Zealand wine industry by empowering our members,” Jelicich said.

“This means giving growers and wineries the information, advocacy and practical support they need to make well-informed decisions.”

Jelicich said NZW’s focus would be on turning the strategy into value for members.

“Our role is to support the industry as a whole so that New Zealand wine can emerge stronger and succeed over the long term”.

content:
Robyn Puglisi-Henderson is now the fourth member of the Puglisi family to receive the award. Images supplied

Robyn Puglisi-Henderson, business manager at Ballandean Estate Wines, has been honoured with the 2026 Samuel Bassett Award at the 42nd Annual Queensland Wine Awards.

The award is the Queensland wine industry’s highest mark of tribute, recognising long-term contribution and leadership.

Puglisi-Henderson is a fourth-generation member of the Puglisi family, the founders and custodians of Queensland’s oldest family-run winery, Ballandean Estate.

She has played a “vital role in the growth and resilience of the business for more than 25 years, since returning to the estate in 1999”.

“Among Robyn’s standout achievements is developing the estate’s export trade from zero to 20 per cent of business turnover in just five years, including establishing a market in China for the Granite Belt’s premium red wine,” said Adam Penberthy, president of the Queensland Wine Industry Association.

“The Samuel Bassett Award celebrates those who believe in what we do, who aren’t afraid to hold our ground in the face of the doubters, and who leave the industry better placed than they found it.”

Robyn with Adam Penberthy, president of the Queensland Wine Industry Association.

With this win, Robyn becomes the fourth member of the Puglisi family to receive the Samuel Bassett Award, following her father Angelo Puglisi (2003), her mother Mary Puglisi (2015) and her sister Leeanne Puglisi-Gangemi (2019).

“We opened the cellar the year I was born. I think I’ve spent more time there talking to people than I have at home! Being part of the Granite Belt’s tourism story for over 50 years is an honour. This week, we saw Stanthorpe awarded Gold at the 2026 Australian Top Tourism Town Awards. What a journey,” exclaimed Robyn Puglisi-Henderson.

“I was raised in a proud winemaking family. and it is my job and my hobby to champion Queensland wine. It is a pleasure to be part of such a great community who share the same passion for premium wine and visitor experiences.”

The winery shared that her work reflects the “essential, often less visible efforts that sustain a regional wine industry: building resilient businesses, creating new markets, supporting people and ensuring that the achievements of one generation become the foundations for the next”. Her contribution to the wider community was also recognised in 2016, when she received a Paul Harris Fellow Award for Community Service.

The Samuel Bassett Award is named for wine industry pioneer Samuel Symons Bassett, who hauled the first wine grape cuttings to Roma in 1863, laying an early foundation for winemaking in Queensland.

content:
Society’s Lee Sangyeop, Loïc Avril, and Yuki Hirose MS were awarded the prestigious Judy Hirst Award. Image credit Marie-Luise Skibbe

The results of Australia’s Wine List of the Year Awards are in, and Melbourne venue Society has been crowned ‘Australia’s Wine List of the Year’. Celebrating its 33rd Anniversary, the Awards ceremony was presented at NSW Parliament House in Sydney where more than 300 industry figures gathered on Monday 28 September.

In addition to the major trophy, Society also picked up another three major titles including ‘Australia’s Best Capital City Dining Wine List’, ‘Best Wine List Victoria’ and ‘Australia’s Best List of Wines by the Glass’. The venue was also a finalist in another three categories: ‘Australia’s Best Listing of Victorian Wines’, ‘Australia’s Best Listing of New Zealand Wines’ and ‘Australia’s Best Listing of Cellared and Museum Wines’. Society’s head sommeliers Loïc Avril, Yuki Hirose MS and sommelier Lee Sangyeop were awarded the prestigious ‘Judy Hirst Award’, which is awarded to the sommeliers responsible for the winning list.

Society’s winning list was praised by chair of judges Toni Paterson MW for its impressive range and versatile offering to cater for those looking for something familiar or new.

“This ranks among Australia’s and the world’s great wine lists, exceptional in its vintage depth and curation and broad in both local and international scope. At heart, it’s a celebration of quality in all its forms,” said Paterson.

“There are close to 90 wines by the glass, ranging from well-priced Australian favourites like MMAD Vineyard Chenin through premium local Chardonnay from By Farr and Tolpuddle to icon reds including Mount Mary Pinot, The Armagh and Grange poured from magnums. Rarities from further afield, including the likes of Benjamin Leroux 1er Cru Meursault or Domaine de la Pousse d’Or Chambolle-Musigny Les Amoureuses, are available as a taste, half-pour or glass.”

Front runners and Hall of Fame inductees

Other front runners for this year’s awards include Perth’s Gibney which was awarded ‘Best Wine List WA’; ‘Australia’s Best Digestif List’, and ‘The Peter Forrestal Award’ for ‘Australia’s Best Listing of Western Australian Wines’. Gibney was also a finalist for four categories including the major title of ‘Australia’s Wine List of the Year 2026’ with judges noting the list’s depth and balance of well-known and up-and-coming producers. Sydney’s Altitude Restaurant at the Shangri-La also took home three titles with judges praising the comprehensive list that also highlights some “left-of-centre” options for those looking to explore.

This year’s state and territory stand-outs included The Boat House (‘Best Wine List ACT’); Shell House Dining Room & Terrace (‘Best Wine List NSW’); Otto Brisbane (‘Best Wine List QLD’); 2KW Bar + Restaurant (‘Best Wine List SA’); and Black Cow Bistro (‘Best Wine List TAS’). It’s the first time Shell House Dining Room & Terrace and 2KW Bar + Restaurant have taken out these major category wins.

“Despite recent challenges, our restaurant sector has great energy, with fabulous wine and beverage lists compiled by confident, knowledgeable sommeliers,” said Paterson of this year’s results.

“The best lists are showing greater support for Australian wines, including those from their home state, which is heartening, especially when local wines represent excellent value, are better than ever, and offer great style and varietal diversity.

“This year has seen the rise of Grenache, mini-cocktails, chilled reds and small pours by the glass, the latter encouraging experimentation while staying mindful of cost. The international offering is incredibly varied, allowing people to explore the world of wine without leaving our shores. We have also seen a wider range of cuisines and menu formats, with share plates increasingly popular.”

Eight venues were also added to the ‘Australia’s Wine List of the Year Awards – Hall of Fame’. To be applicable, venues must have won ‘Australia’s Wine List of the Year’ once or a State/Territory or Australian category award three times while also maintaining their glass rating each year. Among the new inductees for 2026 were Circl (‘Australia’s Wine List of the Year’); Agnes (‘Best Listing of Queensland Wines’ in 2023, 2024, 2025); Fico (‘Best Listing of Tasmanian Wines’ in 2021, 2022, 2025); Settlers Tavern (‘Best Country Restaurant’ in 2022, 2023, 2025); Woodcut (‘Best Hotel List’ in 2023, 2024, 2025); Society (‘Best Listing of French Wines’ in 2023, 2024, 2025); Hardy’s Verandah Restaurant (‘Best Listing of South Australian Wines’ in 2017, 2021, 2025).

Additionally, Amanda Yallop of Fink Group was added to the Hall of Fame. The award is presented periodically to “recognise an outstanding individual and their contribution to industry education, the service of fine wine and the standard of wine lists within the Australian hospitality and tourism industries over recent times”. She is only the third individual in 33 years to receive this honour, joining David Lawler (2018) and Franck Moreau MS (2014).

Founded in 1993

The awards were established in 1993 by Rob Hirst OAM and his late wife, Judy, after whom the main award is named, together with Tucker Seabrook. The awards honour the time, skill, and resources that go into developing the highest-quality wine lists and pay tribute to the talented sommeliers, owners, their teams and the cellars behind them.

“It is wonderful to see the outstanding level of support for the Australia’s Wine List of the Year Awards again this year and the recognition that they deliver to those in the industry continuing to pursue excellence with the list they present to their customers. The quality of wine lists across the country has never been better,” said Hirst.

“These awards are about the recognition and celebration of the outstanding commitment, work and investment of the sommeliers, owners, beverage directors, venue managers and entrepreneurs who make Australia’s hospitality industry one of the best in the world. We congratulate all award winners and glass-rated venues for their achievements this year.”

State highlights

Award organisers have compiled a list of state-by-state highlights:

NSW

New South Wales continued its strong presence in the Awards with a total of 16 major category wins. Altitude Restaurant led the way for the state with three major category wins for ‘Australia’s Best Listing of NSW Wines’, ‘Australia’s Best Listing of Organic and Biodynamic Wines’, and ‘Australia’s Best Hotel/Resort Dining Wine List’. It was also a finalist for ‘Australia’s Best Listing of ACT and Canberra District Wines’ and ‘Australia’s Best Listing of Australian Wines’.

Newcomer Infinity by Mark Best made an impressive debut with two wins: ‘Australia’s Best Listing of Australian Wines’ and ‘The Tony Hitchin Award for Australia’s Best New Wine List’. Hall of Fame member Jonah’s Restaurant and Boutique Hotel continued to make its mark by winning ‘Australia’s Best Food & Wine Matching List’ and the consumer-voted ‘Australia’s Choice Award’.

Shell House Dining Room & Terrace won the overall Award for ‘Best Wine List NSW’, while inner-west favourite ANTE made its debut through the title of ‘Australia’s Best List of Japanese Sake’. Olympus Dining was awarded ‘Australia’s Best Listing of Greek Wines’ for the second year running, and Devine Food & Wine won ‘Australia’s Best Aperitif’ for the third time, previously winning in 2018 and 2024.

Other highlights include Hall of Fame members Rockpool Bar & Grill Sydney acknowledged with ‘Australia’s Best Listing of Cellared and Museum Wines’; The Rover being awarded ‘Australia’s Best Wine List’ (max. 50 Wines) and Me-Gal being named ‘Australia’s Best Wine List’ (max. 100 Wines).

VIC

Victorian venues took out a total of 10 major categories, with Society leading the way through its overall win alongside its titles of ‘Australia’s Best Capital City Dining Wine List’; ‘Best Wine List Victoria’ and ‘Australia’s Best List of Wines by the Glass’. The Mornington Peninsula’s Ten Minutes by Tractor added to its successful history with the Awards by winning ‘Australia’s Best Champagne List’ and ‘Australia’s Best Listing of Victorian Wines’.

Another Mornington Peninsula local, Laura at Pt. Leo Estate, was acknowledged with the title of ‘Australia’s Best Country/Regional Dining Wine List’. Last year’s winner of the ‘Tony Hitchin Award’, Maison Bâtard, was awarded ‘Australia’s Best Listing of French Wines’. Florentino marked its first entry under the stewardship of Edition Hospitality with the win of ‘Australia’s Best Listing of Italian Wines’ while sister venue Reine & La Rue was acknowledged with ‘Australia’s Best Listing of USA Wines’.

WA

Perth’s beachside brasserie Gibney continued its dominance as top performer for the West by taking out ‘Best Wine List WA’; ‘Australia’s Best Digestif List’, and ‘The Peter Forrestal Award for Australia’s Best Listing of Western Australian Wines’. It was also a finalist for four categories including the major title of ‘Australia’s Wine List of the Year 2026’, ‘Australia’s Best Capital City Dining Wine List’, ‘Australia’s Best Champagne List’, and ‘Australia’s Best Cocktail List’.

West Leederville’s neighbourhood pub Besk celebrated back-to-back wins for the title of ‘Australia’s Best Beer List’. Foni Pollitt of Hall of Famers Mayfair Lane Pub & Dining Room was acknowledged by her peers to be awarded the ‘Sommelier’s Choice Award’.

SA

South Australia’s charge was led by The Crafers Hotel which was awarded ‘Australia’s Best Pub Dining Wine List’ and ‘Australia’s Best Listing of South Australian Wine’. 2KW Bar & Restaurant were crowned ‘Best Wine List SA’, with judge Andrew Graham praising the list’s Local Heroes; selection championing cult-status SA producers alongside the up-and-coming.

Adelaide CBD haunt A Prayer for the Wild at Heart received ‘Australia’s Best Wine List’ (max. 200 Wines) for the second year running, while Restaurant Botanic continued its streak of ‘Australia’s Best Non-Alcoholic List’ by winning it for the third year in a row.

Other highlights include CBD venue Canopy acknowledged with ‘Australia’s Best Cocktail List’ plus the Clare Valley’s The Rising Sun made its debut with the title of ‘Australia’s Best Listing of a Single Region’s Wines’.

TAS

Launceston’s Black Cow Bistro received the award for ‘Best Wine List TAS’ with judges noting its diversity in producers and varieties across The Apple Isle. The Agrarian Kitchen in New Norfolk continued its respected celebration of Tasmanian produce by securing the Award for ‘Australia’s Best Listing of Tasmanian Wines’ for the second year in a row and also being named as a finalist for ‘Best Wine List TAS’.

Hobart restaurant Fico was acknowledged as a finalist for ‘Best Wine List TAS’, ‘Australia’s Best Sparkling Wine List’ and ‘Australia’s Best Listing of Tasmanian Wines’. Fellow Hobart local Peppina was also named a finalist for ‘Australia’s Best Hotel/Resort Dining Wine List’ and ‘Best Wine List TAS’.

QLD

Following its six inductions into the Australia’s Wine List of the Year Awards Hall of Fame last year, Cru Bar + Cellar continued its dominance by being named ‘Australia’s Best Sparkling Wine List’ and ‘Australia’s Best Listing of New Zealand’. The Fortitude Valley favourite was also a finalist for ‘Australia’s Best Listing of USA Wines’.

Fink Group’s Otto Brisbane was awarded the overall title of ‘Best Wine List QLD’, while Hall of Famers Blackbird Brisbane was named ‘Australia’s Best Listing of Queensland Wine’ for the second year in a row and a finalist for ‘Australia’s Best Listing of Organic and Biodynamic Wines’.

ACT

Canberran Italian restaurant Capitol Bar & Grill celebrated its win as ‘Australia’s Best Listing of ACT and Canberra District Wines’ for the third consecutive year with judges noting its breadth of local producers from across eight regions. Following its induction into the Hall of Fame last year, The Boat House was awarded the title of ‘Best Wine List ACT’ for its thoughtful selection of benchmarks and newcomers from the area.

The Riesling-led wine bar Rizla was also acknowledged as a finalist for ‘Australia’s Best Wine List’ (max. 200 Wines) and ‘Australia’s Best Listing of ACT and Canberra District Wines’.

content:
The symposium told a consistent message: for businesses and individuals to focus on practical actions within their control. Image credit Robyn Strathearn Photography

Earlier this month, more than 200 professionals from across Australia’s grape and wine community gathered in Melbourne for the 2026 Australian Women in Wine National Symposium, which confronted workforce, leadership and gender-equity challenges as well as shared practical ideas for building a stronger, more inclusive and sustainable industry.

Held under the theme ‘Rising Together – Shaping What Comes Next’, the sell-out event brought together industry leaders, business owners, winemakers, growers, researchers and emerging professionals “to examine the people and leadership challenges facing the sector”.

Organisers said that the conversations were against a backdrop of persistent gender disparities across Australian wine.

According to Wine Australia data, while university wine intakes are close to evenly split between women and men, women represent only around 30% of the sector overall. In key technical roles, the gap is even wider, with women accounting for just 16.7% of winemakers and 21.5% of viticulturists nationally.

Pay disparities also persist, with figures presented during the symposium showing that the average female winemaker earns around $14,000 less per year than the average male winemaker, while female viticulturists earn around $18,000 less per year.

A consistent message emerged throughout the day: “while many of the pressures facing Australian wine are complex, there are practical actions businesses and individuals can take now”.

Australian Women in Wine (AWIW) chair Rachel Triggs said the symposium demonstrated the value of bringing the industry together to move from discussion to practical action.

“What stood out throughout the day was the determination to move beyond talking about the challenges and focus on what we can actually do next.

“Women are entering wine education in almost equal numbers, yet we are still losing too many from the industry before they progress into technical, senior and leadership roles. That tells us the challenge is not simply attracting women to wine, but creating the conditions that allow them to build sustainable, rewarding careers.

“Whether it is leadership, flexibility, workplace culture or opening up new opportunities, meaningful change comes from turning good intentions into practical action,” she said.

Carolyn Creswell, Carman’s Kitchen founder and CEO, was a keynote speaker at the event who challenged delegates to remain customer-focused, create space for innovation and difficult conversations, protect their time and question outdated ways of working.

Her message included a reminder that one of the most dangerous phrases in business is ‘we’ve always done it this way’, and that effective strategy is as much about deciding what not to do, as to what to pursue.

Conversations emphasised the importance of moving beyond policies and commitments to practical implementation. Structural approaches to gender equity, alternative working models including job sharing, and the role supportive workplace cultures can play in attracting and retaining talent were explored throughout discussions.

Lucy Du, representing Global Victoria, spoke about the importance of access to markets, networks, opportunities and decision-making, as well as the value different perspectives and lived experiences bring to leadership. She also highlighted the growing importance of women as consumers in China and the opportunities available to Victorian wine businesses seeking to build international connections.

Closing keynote speaker, Mind Insurance Founder and CEO Mel Neil, focused on “navigating uncertainty by identifying what sits outside our control and where we can have influence”. Delegates were encouraged to direct their energy towards meaningful action, while recognising the role emotional intelligence plays alongside technical capability in leadership, decision-making and team performance, particularly during periods of pressure, change and uncertainty.

The women behind the event

LTR: Luisa Alemao, Lynda Schenk and Chloé James of Purple Giraffe.

Organisers shared exclusively to Daily Wine News that a key force behind the symposium’s success was the partnership between Australian Women in Wine and marketing consultants Purple Giraffe.

Purple Giraffe worked alongside the AWIW team to manage the strategic marketing, communications and event delivery, including coordinating speakers, sponsorship support, stakeholder communications and assets.

Purple Giraffe shared that the project was “an opportunity to apply our strategic marketing expertise to a cause closely aligned with PG’s values: supporting women, leadership and positive change”.

AWIW director Ali Lockwood said the organisation couldn’t have delivered “such a polished, professional and successful event” without the Purple Giraffe team, including marketing consultant Chloé James who led the project.

“From day one, Chloé stepped in with very little notice, quickly got up to speed and took ownership of every detail. Even when things became challenging behind the scenes, she remained calm, organised and completely in control, ensuring everything ran smoothly from start to finish. Beyond her exceptional professionalism, Chloé was an absolute pleasure to work with. Her positive attitude, responsiveness and commitment to excellence made all the difference.

“We were incredibly fortunate to have both Chloé and Purple Giraffe supporting us. Thank you to Chloé, Lynda and the entire Purple Giraffe team for helping make our event such a success.”

content:
The South Australian Government has established an $8 million research and innovation fund for the state’s primary production and forestry sectors, including the wine industry.

The Primary Industries Future Forward Fund will be delivered over four years and support industry-led projects across forestry, livestock, dairy, grains, horticulture, wine, spirits, seafood and fisheries.

The fund will support research and innovation aimed at increasing productivity and capability, building the capacity of primary producers to respond to environmental and market pressures, improving sustainability throughout supply chains, strengthening the primary industries workforce, and improving preparedness for environmental disruptions, biosecurity threats and other emerging issues.

The government said projects should also align with relevant industry masterplans, blueprints or other strategic plans and reports, including the South Australian Wine Industry Association’s Key Priorities 2025-2028 and the Wine Grape Council SA Strategic Plan 2025-2027.

Australian Wine Research Institute managing director Dr Mark Krstic said innovation is important for the South Australian wine industry as it responds to difficult market conditions.

“The wine industry globally is facing significant headwinds at present. Investing in innovation is key to supporting the South Australian wine industry to adapt and thrive again in these challenging market conditions.

“The South Australian Government has a strong history of backing its primary producers to develop and adopt world-leading science and industry innovations.”

The $8 million Future Forward Fund is additional to the South Australian Government’s $50 million Research and Productivity Fund included in the 2026-27 state budget, with the Future Forward Fund specifically targeted at primary industries and forestry.

South Australian Minister for Primary Industries and Regional Development Clare Scriven said the fund is intended to support industry-led research and innovation.

“The Primary Industries Future Forward Fund is about backing agricultural research and innovation that is industry-led and aimed at advancing primary production and forestry in our state.”

The fund follows the 150th anniversary of the invention of the stump-jump plough by Yorke Peninsula brothers Richard and Clarence Smith, which the government describes as an example of South Australia’s history of agricultural innovation.

Applications and guidelines for the Primary Industries Future Forward Fund are available at pir.sa.gov.au/future-forward-fund.

The 2026 Orange Wine Show results were announced yesterday at the Orange Wine Show Lunch held at the Department of Primary Industries.

This year’s show received 290 entries, which organisers said reflects “the growth and maturity of the region”.

“The quality of wines from the Orange region is showing continuous improvement and these wines are seriously competitive on the highest stages,” said chair of judges Mike De Iuliis, who also recently chaired the 200th Sydney Royal Wine Show.

“Particular highlights included the region’s Chardonnay, Sparkling and Pinot Noir. These varieties are fast becoming the wines on which the region can hang its hat.

“The Chardonnay is undeniably world class and the diversity of styles from the region shines a light on the differing terroir and skill of winemakers in Orange.”

Of the entries, 26 wines were awarded gold medals, 57 silver and 97 bronze.

The 2026 Orange Wine Show trophy winners are as follows:

Impresstik Labelling Systems Best Wine of Show

  • Byrne Farm ‘Single Barrel’ Chardonnay 2024

ICC Sydney Best Exhibitor of Show

  • Swinging Bridge Wines

Quest Orange Best Single Vineyard Wine of Show

  • Byrne Farm ‘Single Barrel’ Chardonnay 2024

Define Wine Marketing & Communications Best Red Wine of Show

  • Angullong Pinot Noir 2025

Classic Oak Products Best White Wine of Show

  • Byrne Farm ‘Single Barrel’ Chardonnay 2024

Orange 360 Wine of Provenance 

  • Swinging Bridge ‘Hill Park’ Chardonnay

The Lane Cellars Best Sparkling Wine

  • Zinga ‘Bianco d’Bianco’ Chardonnay 2021

  • Tamburlaine Organic Wines Sauvignon Blanc 2026

Define Wine Marketing & Communications Best Chardonnay 2025 or 2026

  • Swinging Bridge ‘Hill Park’ Chardonnay 2025

Classic Oak Products Best Chardonnay 2022 to 2024

Barrack Broking Best Mature White Wine

  • See Saw ‘Fulcra’ Chardonnay 2021

Ace Ohlsson Best Rosé

Byrne Farm Best Pinot Noir
